summary: Jude opens by greeting believers as called, sanctified, and kept, then says he has changed his intended subject in order to urge them to contend for the faith. Most of the chapter denounces certain people within the community through examples of judgment, warnings about speech and desire, and a rush of images. The ending turns directly to the beloved readers: remember the apostles' words, build yourselves up, show discerning mercy, and trust God to keep and present them with joy.
whyItMatters: This one-chapter letter shows its warning and its pastoral purpose together: danger is named sharply, but the readers' response is perseverance, prayer, mercy, and confidence in God. It also matters because Jude draws on Jewish scriptural and traditional material, so careful reading must distinguish what the chapter says from later debates about those sources.

context.author: The writer names himself Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James. Tradition connects him with Jesus's family, while some readers propose a later writer using Jude's name.
context.audience: Believers addressed as called, sanctified by God the Father, and kept for Jesus Christ; their city or congregation is not named.
context.date: Often placed in the later first century, with some proposals extending into the early second; the date remains uncertain and tied to authorship.
context.setting: A Christian community familiar with Israel's scriptures and Jewish traditions, facing people Jude says have entered its shared life and love feasts.
context.literaryForm: A short letter of warning and exhortation, moving from greeting and occasion to examples, accusations, direct counsel, and closing praise.

outline.heading: Greeting to the kept
outline.note: Jude identifies himself and blesses the readers with mercy, peace, and love.

outline.heading: The reason for writing
outline.note: A planned letter about common salvation becomes an urgent appeal to contend for the delivered faith because certain men have crept in.

outline.heading: Remembered judgments
outline.note: The chapter recalls unbelieving people after Egypt, angels who abandoned their domain, and Sodom and Gomorrah as examples of judgment.

outline.heading: Accusations and warnings
outline.note: Jude charges the opponents with defilement, contempt for authority, abusive speech, and self-interest, using examples and vivid images.

outline.heading: The beloved readers' response
outline.note: The readers are told to remember apostolic warnings, build themselves up, pray, keep themselves in God's love, look for mercy, and help others with discernment.

outline.heading: Praise to the God who keeps
outline.note: The letter closes by praising God as able to keep and present his people faultless with joy.

keyVerses.text: Beloved, while I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation, I was constrained to write to you exhorting you to contend earnestly for the faith which was once for all delivered to the saints.
keyVerses.why: This verse states the occasion and purpose of the letter: Jude's intended topic gives way to an urgent appeal about the received faith.

keyVerses.text: For there are certain men who crept in secretly, even those who were long ago written about for this condemnation: ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into indecency, and denying our only Master, God, and Lord, Jesus Christ.
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the central charge against the people Jude denounces, before the examples and images expand the warning.

keyVerses.text: But you, beloved, keep building up yourselves on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit.
keyVerses.why: This renewed address to the beloved calls for building up and prayer, making the community's positive response explicit alongside Jude's warnings.

keyVerses.text: Now to him who is able to keep them from stumbling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory in great joy,
keyVerses.why: The closing praise answers the chapter's danger with confidence in God's ability to guard and present his people.

questions.question: Who is Jude in this letter?
questions.answer: The chapter names him as "Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James." Tradition identifies him with the Jude named among Jesus's relatives, while another proposal is that a later writer used Jude's name. The opening gives the writer's claimed identity without independently resolving that historical question.

questions.question: Who are the readers?
questions.answer: They are addressed as people who are called, sanctified by God the Father, and kept for Jesus Christ. The letter later calls them beloved and speaks to them as a community that can remember apostolic words, build itself up, pray, and show mercy. No city, region, or congregation name is given in the chapter.

questions.question: What does Jude mean by "contend earnestly"?
questions.answer: Verse 3 urges the readers to contend earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints. The later commands give that response practical shape: remember, build up, pray, keep yourselves in God's love, look for mercy, and help others. The struggle language expresses urgency; the chapter directs it toward faithfulness and care within the community.

questions.question: What is the main accusation against the people Jude denounces?
questions.answer: Verse 4 says they turn the grace of God into indecency and deny the only Master, God, and Lord, Jesus Christ. The later verses add charges about defiling the flesh, despising authority, slandering celestial beings, speaking evil, pursuing gain, causing divisions, and lacking the Spirit. These are Jude's accusations; the opponents' own account is not preserved in the chapter.

questions.question: Why does Jude bring up Egypt, angels, and Sodom and Gomorrah?
questions.answer: Jude recalls rescue followed by judgment on unbelief, angels kept for judgment after abandoning their domain, and Sodom and Gomorrah under punishment. These remembered examples support his present warning without forming one continuous story. In verse 5, WEB reads the Lord, while Douay-Rheims and the SBL Greek text read Jesus; that difference reflects a variant reading.

questions.question: What is happening with Michael, the devil, and Moses's body?
questions.answer: Verse 9 refers to Michael the archangel disputing with the devil about the body of Moses. This tradition is commonly associated with the Assumption of Moses; it is not an episode narrated in Deuteronomy. Jude uses Michael's restraint to challenge abusive speech: the archangel does not bring an abusive condemnation but says, "May the Lord rebuke you!"

questions.question: Why does Jude quote Enoch?
questions.answer: Verses 14–15 quote 1 Enoch 1:9 as a prophecy of judgment on ungodly deeds and harsh speech. Jude applies that announced judgment to the people he denounces, treating Enoch's words as a witness in his argument. Quoting this passage does not by itself settle the canonical status of the whole book of 1 Enoch.

questions.question: What are the readers supposed to do after hearing all these warnings?
questions.answer: Jude turns to "you, beloved" and tells them to remember the apostles' words. He then tells them to keep building themselves up on their most holy faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep themselves in God's love, look for the mercy of Jesus Christ, and show compassion or rescue others with discernment and fear. The response is active, but it is not the same as imitating the abusive speech Jude condemns.

questions.question: Why do verses 22-23 sound difficult to apply?
questions.answer: WEB gives two groups: some receive compassion, and some are rescued from the fire with fear. Douay-Rheims and the SBL Greek text distinguish three groups, with differences in the verbs as well. These variants affect how the instructions are divided. The fire and stained-clothing images hold rescue and caution together: readers must help others while remaining alert to the wrongdoing Jude condemns.

glossary.def: A direct address Jude uses for the readers when he explains why he is writing and when he turns from denunciation to their response.
The shared salvation Jude first wanted to write about before he says he was constrained to write an urgent appeal.
Community meals where Jude says the denounced people are present and self-serving.
Heavenly beings whom Jude says the opponents slander. Michael's restrained speech in verse 9 supplies the contrast.
Falling into wrongdoing or failing to remain faithful, pictured as a misstep. The closing praise credits God with guarding against it.

reviewer: Codex editorial panel (3 John, Jude, Haggai)
